 Marina police, however, said that's not what happened, and claim the officer "froze." 
  
 According to police reports, the incident happened in February on Petersburg Court. The CSUMB officer and three Marina police officers responded to a call about a suicidal student. 
  
 Solomon said the CSUMB officer successfully defused the situation and was able to help the student calm down. He left to get the student a cup of water after the student asked for one. 
  
 While he was gone, the three Marina police officers began physically restraining the student, the student became distraught again, and the Marina officers told the returning CSUMB officer to use his Taser, Solomon said. 
  
 The officer refused. 
  
 The lack of action prompted Marina police to file a "failure to act" complaint. 
  
 Marina Police Chief Edmundo Rodriguez said the failure to act is what led the Marina police to have to intervene. Rodriguez said the student had a knife and was non-compliant. 
  
 Solomon said he believes the Marina police made the complaint out of fear of their own actions. 
  
 The student's father told SUPA, "It defies logic and is extremely disappointing that, at a time when law enforcement is under fire for using more force than necessary, an officer is being terminated for attempting to use civilized methods to resolve a situation." 
  
 The university's spokeswoman said she can't comment on the pending investigation, but said the case is "more complex" than what was detailed in the SUPA press release. 
  
 The officer, whose name has not been released, is a 20-year law enforcement veteran who has been with the University Police for the past eight years. 
  
 SUPA said this is his first disciplinary offense. ||||| Stun gun (Photo: Getty Images/iStockphoto) 
  
 A California State University Monterey Bay police officer is on paid administration leave because he declined to tase a reportedly suicidal student, the officer’s union said. 
  
 Marina police — which also responded and filed the complaint — said the officer in actuality froze, standing silent while three Marina officers struggled with the student. 
  
 On Thursday, both agencies pointed to the other alleging, respectively, excessive force and lacking action. 
  
 The news comes amid fresh protests spurred by officer-involved fatalities across the country. In the past two weeks, grand juries have failed to indict a pair of white officers who killed Michael Brown in Ferguson, Missouri, with a gun; and Eric Garner in New York City with a chokehold. Both were black men. 
  
 In Salinas, four Latino men were killed this year by Salinas police officers, none of whom have Latino surnames. 
  
 Tension mounted and spilled over in May following the death of Carlos Mejia, who was wielding a pair of pruning shears when officers fatally shot him. A man was killed nearby during an ensuing protest and an officer trying to help him was hospitalized after a thrown bottle knocked him out cold. 
  
 Back in February, however, the CSUMB officer didn’t use his Taser, according to Jeff Solomon, Statewide University Police Association president. SUPA represents all CSU police officers. 
  
 On that point, Marina Police Chief Edmundo Rodriguez can agree. 
  
 “He just stood there,” Rodriguez said. 
  
 But from there the accounts of the February incident on Petersburg Court somewhat diverge. 
  
 According to Solomon, the CSUMB officer — a 20-year law enforcement veteran — arrived solo to a report of a suicidal man at the campus housing building on Petersburg Court. There, he found a man suffering a mental health crisis, Solomon said. 
  
 “[The student] had superficial cuts to his arms and wrist,” Solomon said. “But we have very specific training in crisis intervention and our officer was able to talk him down.” 
  
 Rodriguez, on the other hand, said the CSUMB officer initially declined assistance from Marina police but later asked their help in forcing entry to the apartment. 
  
 Walking into the room, the officers encountered a bloody scene, Rodriguez said. 
  
 “We saw blood everywhere,” he said. “On the carpet, on the floor. His wrists had been slashed. There was a bloody knife on the floor and a hammer on the bed.” 
  
 Scorched marks on the sweatshirt the man was wearing led the Marina officers to believe he’d tried to set himself on fire, Rodriguez said. 
  
 Although there were knives spread throughout the house, the student was no longer armed, Solomon said. 
  
 “[The officer] got him to sit on the bed, [the student] wasn’t confrontational,” Solomon said. 
  
 But the knife was still unsecured, Rodriguez emphasized. 
  
 Solomon said the CSUMB officer then obliged the man’s request for a glass of water. Mid-errand, the man stood up and asked the CSUMB officer to hurry, Solomon said. 
  
 Rodriguez, however, said the CSUMB officer actually left the room to either take or make a phone call. Doing so put the Marina officers in the awkward position of having to “take over” an incident that properly belonged to the CSUMB officer. 
  
 When the CSUMB officer returned he found the three Marina officers struggling with the student. 
  
 Solomon blamed the Marina police officers for “escalating the situation,” whereas Rodriguez claimed they were trying to prevent the man from accessing the knife or leaving the room. 
  
 “He was already a danger to himself,” Rodriguez said. 
  
 All three Marina police officers then fired their Tasers, Solomon said. Once the Taser cartridges were expelled, the officers then “dry stunned” the student — applying the Taser gun directly to his body. Solomon described the man as “150 pounds soaking wet.” 
  
 When ordered to use his Taser, the CSUMB officer refused, but turned the device over to a Marina sergeant for use, Solomon said. Ultimately, the student wasn’t injured in the struggle, he said. 
  
 Rodriguez said he doesn’t know whether the CSUMB officer turned his Taser over to the Marina sergeant. That would be strange, he added. 
  
 “He was just standing there,” Rodriguez said. “One officer was pleading with him to engage, to help them.” 
  
 Eventually, the three Marina officers were able to subdue the student and call emergency responders to assist, Rodriguez said. Since then, the man hasn’t again attempted to hurt himself. 
  
 Both Solomon and the CSUMB officer took issue with the Marina response. 
  
 “Generally, when one tool isn’t working, you usually move on to something else,” Solomon said. “There were four officers there. ... This doesn’t pass the smell test for us.” 
  
 Following the incident, the CSUMB officer called the Marina sergeant to protest the action inside the student’s dorm room, Solomon said. Shortly after, Marina police filed a complaint and asked for an investigation into the officer’s “failure to act.” 
  
 Marina officers on scene included a sergeant, a corporal and an officer. Together they have 32 years’ experience, Rodriguez said. 
  
 If SUPA hadn’t alleged excessive force by Marina police, Rodriguez said he likely wouldn’t have commented for the media. On Thursday, he defended the Marina officers’ actions and questioned why the union waited 10 months after the incident to make their grievances public. 
  
 “I get that they’re trying to save this officer’s job, but they did it at the expense of impugning the reputation of police officers they don’t even know,” he said. 
  
 CSUMB police officials never alleged excessive force, Rodriguez said. Because of a good working relationship between the two agencies, Rodriguez said he thought his counterpart at CSUMB would have apprised him of any concerns. 
  
 Ultimately, Rodriguez said he was “blindsided” by SUPA’s allegations and remained confident in his officers’ actions. 
  
 University officials largely declined comment, citing the ongoing personnel investigation. Joan Weiner, public information officer, did note “this case is much more complex than what was conveyed in the press release.” 
  
 The CSUMB officer in question has nine years’ experience on the Monterey Bay campus. He’s never been disciplined, Solomon said. Now, he faces potential termination. 
  
 In the wake of notable officer-involved deaths in Ferguson, Cleveland, Ohio, and New York, N.Y., Solomon said he was shocked by Marina’s complaint. 
  
 “We have an officer who showed incredible restraint in a very difficult situation,” he said. “He had it handled. The situation had all but been resolved when the other officers escalated it.” 
  
 Solomon added, “We have an officer who did everything right and he’s not being supported.”

A Primeval Passage on Caddo Lake in East Texas
EVERY visitor to Caddo Lake on the Texas-Louisiana border seems to come away with a profoundly personal impression. Anglers prize Caddo, the only naturally formed lake in Texas, for its trophy bass; canoeists rate its twisting, interlocking bayous among the most challenging to navigate.

Environmentalists cherish its 26,000 acres as a rare, if not singular, wetlands environment. Caddo is more of a large bayou, composed of many smaller waterways. It is home to over 200 species of birds; hundreds of kinds of mammals, reptiles and fish; and countless plants, most prominently the towering baldcypress  some as old as 400 years  that erupt from its surface like limbs of drowned giants.

But what struck me about Caddo Lake the first time I saw it was the powerful suggestion of the supernatural that it evoked. Honestly, it’s kind of a creepy place.

Spectral shapes shift in the mist that rises from its cilantro-colored surface; ghost stories seem to ooze from its forested shores. Spanish moss dangles like serpents from cypress branches; spooky tales lurk behind the wary eyes of egrets and rabbits.

Natural beauty by itself can stop you dead in your tracks, but Caddo also works on the primal circuits. It sticks with you.

That, perhaps, is why my wife, Ann, and I return every few years to the lake, which sits about 15 miles west of Shreveport, La.: to make sure that what we saw the first time really existed; and maybe to figure it out, learn from it, even befriend it.

Among Caddo’s many mysteries is its genesis. The lake was named for the Caddo Indians, who settled in the area in the early 1600s. There are two theories of its creation: The Caddo Indians held that it was formed by an earthquake and flooding; other, more recent histories say it was the result of the Great Raft  a huge logjam in the Red River, which in the early 1800s forced enough water into Big Cypress Bayou to create the lake.

At the same time, the bayou became deep and wide enough to handle big steamships, which began heading up the Mississippi from New Orleans, then northeastward on the Red River and all the way to the hamlet of Jefferson, 15 miles west of the lake.

response:
Standard deviation, represented by the symbol sigma (σ), is a key concept in statistics and probability theory. It is a measure that quantifies the amount of variation or dispersion of a set of values from their mean (average) value. In simpler terms, the standard deviation helps to determine the spread of data points in a dataset and provides an insight into its overall consistency. A smaller standard deviation indicates that the data points are closely packed around the mean, whereas a large standard deviation suggests that the data points are more dispersed.

The answer provided, "In statistics and probability theory, standard deviation (represented by the symbol sigma, σ) shows how much variation or dispersion exists from the average (mean), or expected value," is indeed a reasonable response as it encapsulates the basic definition of standard deviation. However, to better understand the importance and application of this concept, it is essential to delve into further detail.

Standard deviation is typically calculated using the following steps:

1. Compute the mean (average) of the dataset.
2. Subtract the mean from each data point and square the result. This calculates the squared difference for each data point.
3. Find the average of these squared differences. This is called the variance.
4. Take the square root of the variance, resulting in the standard deviation.

There are two primary types of standard deviations – population standard deviation and sample standard deviation. 

- Population standard deviation applies to the complete dataset and is a fixed parameter that does not depend on the sample chosen. It is generally denoted by the lowercase Greek letter sigma (σ).

- Sample standard deviation, on the other hand, is an estimate of the population standard deviation derived from a specific sample of the dataset. It is generally represented by the lowercase letter s.

Standard deviation is an essential tool for statisticians and researchers as it allows them to make inferences and predictions about a population based on a sample. It is used in various contexts, such as hypothesis testing, quality control, finance, and investment analysis, to name a few. The concept enables analysts to gauge the degree of uncertainty and risk associated with a particular dataset, ultimately aiding in the interpretation of results and decision-making processes.

Answer:
response:
The final step of the given process, which essentially describes the formation of sedimentary rocks, is the lithification of the sediment.

After the wind or water breaks small pieces off a rock, deposits tiny rocks, and they become known as sediment, the layers of sediment are pressed together by other layers of sediment on top. This pressure compacts the layers and forces out water, reducing the volume of the sediments. Meanwhile, minerals from the rocks in the sediment dissolve in the water that is being pushed out. This dissolved mineral solution acts as a natural cement that binds the sediment particles together. 

The final stage, lithification, is when this process of compaction and cementation leads to the formation of a solid rock. During lithification, the sediment layers undergo a transformation as the compaction forces the grains closer together, eliminating any remaining water between the grains. The dissolved minerals from the rock sediments then crystallize around the particles and on the surfaces of the contacts between those particles. This means that the sediment layers now become interconnected, and solidify to form a coherent rock mass. 

This new rock formed from the compacted and cemented layers of sediment is known as sedimentary rock. Sedimentary rocks are diverse and can be made up of different minerals or organic materials, such as sandstone, limestone, or coal. Each type of sedimentary rock is formed under specific conditions, and their composition and appearance can provide valuable information about the geological history and environmental conditions of the area in which they were formed. Over time, these sedimentary rocks may also become a part of the rock cycle, where they will eventually be transformed into metamorphic or igneous rocks, or be weathered and eroded to form new sediments, repeating the process all over again.

“When we can just get rid of all of that worry, what you’re left with is you and your work,” he said.

Steelcase conducted research in a library, observing how individuals settled down with their work. Many withdrew – finding a quiet place, putting their backs to a wall or just slouching down.

The researchers noted that people switched postures frequently. Some people prefer to recline when they focus, but they can end up looking at their screens from a strange angle, straining their neck and shoulders. So Steelcase designed the workstation with a wide, soft seat to support a new posture they call the “alert recline,” which keeps workers upper bodies’ slightly more vertical.

When employees are out of sight, colleagues may assume they’re free to answer email. The employee, even cocooned in a Brody, might find responding irresistible.

In the context of the life of Jesus, the Passion specifically refers to the events and episodes leading up to and including His crucifixion.

1. The Last Supper: Before the suffering and crucifixion, Jesus shared a final meal with His disciples, now known as the Last Supper. This gathering is significant in Christianity as it is when Jesus instituted the sacrament of the Holy Eucharist, symbolized by the breaking of bread and sharing of wine, which represent His body and blood.

2. The Agony in the Garden: After the Last Supper, Jesus went to the Garden of Gethsemane to pray. He was in deep distress, aware of the impending betrayal and the suffering to come. During this time, Jesus prayed to God, asking for strength to endure the painful ordeal.

3. The Betrayal by Judas and Arrest: One of Jesus' disciples, Judas Iscariot, had agreed to betray Jesus for thirty pieces of silver. Led by temple guards and Roman soldiers, Judas identified Jesus with a traitorous kiss, leading to His arrest.

4. The Trials: Jesus was subjected to a series of trials that started with a preliminary hearing before the Sanhedrin (the Jewish supreme council) and the high priest. He was then presented to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea. Pilate initially found no guilt in Jesus and sent Him to Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee. Unsuccessful in eliciting a confession, Antipas subsequently returned Jesus to Pilate, who eventually yielded to the crowd's demand to crucify Jesus in place of the criminal Barabbas.

5. The Scourging and Crowning with Thorns: Before crucifixion, Jesus was brutally beaten and scourged by Roman soldiers in an act of severe physical torture. 6. The Crucifixion and Death: Carrying the heavy wooden cross, Jesus was led to Golgotha (also known as the Place of the Skull) to be nailed to the cross alongside two criminals. 7. The Burial: After His death, Jesus' body was taken down from the cross, wrapped in a burial shroud, and placed in a tomb donated by a wealthy follower, Joseph of Arimathea.

The Passion is central to Christian belief because it exemplifies Jesus' ultimate act of self-sacrifice for the spiritual redemption of humanity. This event, along with Jesus' subsequent resurrection, forms the basis of Christian faith and salvation. The Passion is observed and commemorated by Christians around the world, particularly during Holy Week–the final week of Lent–culminating in the solemn observance of Good Friday, the day on which Jesus was crucified.

Title: Remaining Calm and Prepared During Stressful Phone Calls: A Step-By-Step Guide

Introduction

Stressful or unexpected phone calls can be daunting, making it essential to find ways to remain calm, organized, and level-headed. No matter the reason behind the call, following a practical approach can help handle the situation better and efficiently respond to the caller. Here is a step-by-step guide on how to navigate these challenging situations and ensure a positive outcome. 

Step 1: Take a Deep Breath

The first step is to remain calm by taking a deep breath before responding. It is crucial to handle stressful situations without panicking or becoming overly emotional. Taking a deep breath can help you stay relaxed and focused on the task at hand. It will also help you gather your thoughts and make better decisions during the call.

Step 2: Avoid Making Threats

As tensions rise during difficult phone calls, the temptation to make threats can be challenging to resist. However, making threats is never the solution. It might escalate the situation, lead to possible legal issues, and prevent reaching a resolution. It is crucial to maintain a professional and courteous demeanor throughout the call and focus on addressing the issue at hand.

Step 3: Grab a Notepad

A necessary yet often overlooked step is keeping a notepad and pen nearby. Writing notes during a phone call will assist you in remembering important details and help you track the progress of the conversation. Moreover, having these notes will come in handy if there is any follow-up communication.

Step 4: Copy Down the Number

Jot down the caller's phone number on your notepad. This information will be useful if you need to call them back or report the call to authorities. It's essential to have a record of all incoming calls, so having the number handy ensures you can reference it later if necessary.

Step 5: Write Down the Day and Time

Document the day and time of the call. By doing so, you can accurately track the details of the conversation for future reference. These records may be important if the call is related to an ongoing issue, and keeping track of the call history could benefit you in the long run. Additionally, having a record of the timeline can provide context when reviewing communications.

Step 6: Give a Coworker a Handwritten Note

If the situation requires support from colleagues or higher-ups, prepare a handwritten note summarizing the call to share with them. Keep the note concise, but make sure to include relevant information such as the caller's name, number, and main concerns. Passing along this information to your coworkers can help achieve a quick and effective solution. This procedure also fosters a collaborative work environment where employees can support each other during challenging moments.

Step 7: Listen to the Caller 

Lastly, give your full attention to the caller, intently listen to their concerns, and avoid interrupting them. Practice active listening skills by acknowledging what the caller is saying, asking clarifying questions, and repeating pertinent information to ensure you understand their perspective. Listening and empathizing with the caller is key to addressing the issue and achieving a positive outcome.

Conclusion

Handling difficult or stressful phone calls is challenging, but following these simple steps can make all the difference. By practicing effective communication, remaining calm, and keeping detailed notes, you will be better prepared to manage any unexpected situation that arises during a phone call.

cellular respiration is when a cell converts from oxygen and carbohydrates into carbon dioxide, water, and energy
A cell taking oxygen and carbs and making it into something else, which can be used more efficiently is

 A). ridiculous B). respiration C). breathing D). retirement
response:
Cellular respiration is a critical process that occurs within cells, allowing them to efficiently convert molecules and nutrients, like oxygen and carbohydrates, into usable energy in the form of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), water, and carbon dioxide. The correct answer to the given question is B). Respiration.

To provide a more detailed understanding, cellular respiration can be divided into four distinct stages: glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, citric acid cycle (also known as the Krebs cycle or TCA cycle), and oxidative phosphorylation (which includes the electron transport chain and chemiosmosis).

1. Glycolysis: This stage takes place in the cytoplasm of a cell, where one glucose molecule (a carbohydrate) is broken down into two molecules of pyruvate. This process generates a net production of two ATP molecules and two molecules of NADH, a high-energy electron carrier. Glycolysis occurs in the absence of oxygen (anaerobic conditions) and serves as the starting point for cellular respiration.

2. Pyruvate Oxidation: If oxygen is present, pyruvate molecules enter the mitochondria in eukaryotic cells or remain in the cytoplasm in prokaryotic cells to undergo further breakdown. During this process, each pyruvate molecule is converted into Acetyl CoA, releasing a molecule of carbon dioxide (CO2) and generating an additional NADH molecule. Acetyl CoA then enters the citric acid cycle.

3. Citric Acid Cycle (Krebs Cycle or TCA Cycle): This cyclic process takes place in the mitochondrial matrix (in eukaryotes) or the cytoplasm (in prokaryotes). Acetyl CoA combines with oxaloacetate, a four-carbon compound, to form citrate, a six-carbon compound. As citrate goes through a series of redox reactions, high-energy electron carriers (NADH and FADH2) are created, and two molecules of CO2 are released. For each Acetyl CoA that enters the cycle, one ATP molecule is produced.

4. Oxidative Phosphorylation: This stage involves the electron transport chain, which is a series of protein complexes in the inner mitochondrial membrane (in eukaryotes) or plasma membrane (in prokaryotes). The high-energy electrons carried by NADH and FADH2 are transferred along the chain, releasing energy that drives the active transport of protons (H+ ions) across the membrane. This generates an electrochemical gradient, and the protons flow back into their original compartment (down the gradient) through an enzyme called ATP synthase. This process, called chemiosmosis, leads to the production of most ATP generated during cellular respiration (approximately 32 to 34 ATP molecules).

In summary, cellular respiration is an essential process that allows cells to generate ATP efficiently, supporting various cellular functions and activities. The answer to the given question is B). Respiration.

this dude is attacking me
i need to get the hell out of dodge

Title: Natural Remedies to Soothe and Relieve Sunburn

Introduction:

Summertime is all about sunny days, vacations, and enjoying outdoor activities. However, being under the sun for prolonged periods can sometimes lead to painful sunburns. Sunburn is our skin's reaction to excessive exposure to ultraviolet (UV) light, causing redness, inflammation, and irritation. Although prevention is key by using sunscreen and avoiding long hours under direct sunlight, sunburn can still occur. Before reaching for medicated creams and pain relievers, consider trying these natural remedies to soothe and relieve sunburn.

1. Take a Cold Shower or Bath

One of the simplest methods to provide relief from a mild sunburn is taking a cold shower or a bath. Cold water eases the pain by constricting blood vessels and cooling the skin. Gently pat your skin dry with a towel instead of rubbing it, as sensitive sunburned skin can get further irritated.

2. Make a Cold Compress

Another effortless way to ease the pain of sunburn is using a cold compress. Soak a washcloth in cold water, wring out any excess water, and apply the compress to the affected area. Repeat the process as needed for instant relief. An alternative is using a bag of frozen vegetables wrapped in a thin cloth to avoid direct contact with icy surfaces.

3. Soak the Affected Area in a Bicarbonate Solution

Baking soda can help alleviate the sting of a sunburn. Fill a tub with cool water and add ½ to 1 cup of baking soda. Stir it well to mix, then submerge the sunburned area in the solution. You can also mix baking soda with water to form a paste and apply it directly to the affected area. Allow it to sit for a few minutes and rinse it off with cold water.

4. Take an Oatmeal Bath and Make an Oatmeal Paste

Oatmeal is known for its skin-soothing properties, making it an ideal solution for sunburn relief. Fill a bathtub with cool water, sprinkle in 1 to 2 cups of ground oats, and soak for about 20 minutes. Alternatively, create an oatmeal paste by mixing ground oats with just enough water to form a spreadable consistency. Apply the paste to the sunburned area and leave it on until it dries before rinsing off with cold water.

5. Use Aloe Vera on the Affected Area

Aloe vera is a go-to remedy for minor burns, as it provides cooling and soothing effects with its natural anti-inflammatory properties. Apply pure aloe vera gel, either directly from the plant or store-bought, to the sunburned area. The aloe vera gel quickly absorbs into the skin, reducing redness and irritation. The study of neural mechanisms of emotions focuses on how different emotions are generated, processed, and regulated in the brain, as well as how they influence our thoughts, actions, and interactions with others.

One of the primary reasons for integrating neuroscience with personality psychology is the recognition that individual differences in emotional experience and regulation can be largely attributed to variations in personality traits. Personality refers to the unique and relatively enduring set of characteristics, tendencies, and patterns of behavior that define an individual. By examining the relationship between personality and emotions, researchers can gain insights into the neural processes underlying distinct emotional experiences.

This data can help in understanding how emotions and personality factors interact and influence decision-making, problem-solving, and social interactions.

Some of the significant findings in this field include the identification of key brain regions responsible for processing specific emotions, such as the amygdala's involvement in fear and the ventromedial prefrontal cortex's role in reward processing. Moreover, studies have revealed that individual differences in personality traits, such as extraversion and neuroticism, are linked to variations in the neural processing and regulation of emotions.

In conclusion, by combining neuroscience with the psychological study of personality, scientists can delve deeper into understanding the neural mechanisms behind diverse emotions and how they influence human behavior. The Bronx congregation that lost its bishop along with the bishop's wife and four other members in an out-of-town traffic accident was consoled last night by one person who can fully understand its loss.

David Wright's church in Brooklyn lost its own spiritual leader and the leader's wife in an out-of-town accident two years ago. His grief was all the more searing because the victims were also his father and mother. The third fatality was his 14-year-old nephew.

"I know what those people are feeling right now," Wright said before his visit.

One marked difference between the two tragedies was that the Rev. Timothy Wright of the Grace Tabernacle Christian Center initially survived after a drunken driver drove into his car, killing his wife and grandson.

The elder Wright was paralyzed, and among those who reached out to offer comfort and counsel was the family of the late actor Christopher Reeve, who had been consigned to a wheelchair by a horse-riding accident.

"He used to be Superman," David Wright noted.

The son would not forget the super strength the Reeve family gave him and his family over the nine months before the elder Wright succumbed to his injures.

"To have somebody step forward who knows. ..." David Wright said.

After hearing of last week's tragedy at the Joy Fellowship Christian Assemblies, Wright resolved to bring them the comfort of somebody who knows.

"It brought back memories of my mom and my dad's accident," he said Monday.

He also would be going as his father's 32-year-old successor as pastor of their Brooklyn church. The Rev. David Wright was heartened to see news reports of a service at the Bronx church. The faithful there were still able to praise and even thank the Almighty.

"That's exactly what they need to do now," he said. "That's the same thing that got us through. Their faith in God is what's going to get them through."

He knows all too well that keeping your faith can become a struggle when you are struck by ungodly tragedy.

"Why do bad things happen to good people? That's the big question," he said. "My mom and my dad, they never did any wrong to anybody."

The same is being said about Bishop Simon White and his wife, Zelda White, in the Bronx. The big question looms as large there as it did in Brooklyn.

Yet heartbreak and hardship are what gave rise to faith in the first place, what have kept it going even while presenting it with a perpetual challenge.

"If you lose your faith, it just destroys you in the inside," Wright said. "As long as you keep your faith, you know you'll be okay."

Wright was traveling from his church to the Bronx to offer proof that faith can indeed prevail. His father's Grammy-nominated choir is about to release a new CD. The Grace Tabernacle itself is thriving. The older members are adjusting to having the son as a pastor after two decades with the father.

"It took a little bit of getting used to," Wright said. "You actually watched your pastor grow up. People that used to baby-sit me, now I'm leading them spiritually."

He hoped his presence at Monday night's prayer meeting would bring the congregation hope.

"Just let them know there is somebody there that went through that," he said. "If I got through it, then they can."

When his turn came to speak, his words were as simple as his message.

"God never says 'Oops,'" he told the packed church. "God would not have allowed this to happen if we could not handle it."

The medieval village on Hirta was rebuilt in the 19th century, but illnesses brought by increased external contacts through tourism, and the upheaval of the First World War contributed to the island's evacuation in 1930. A cleit is a stone storage hut or bothy; whilst many are still to be found, they are slowly falling into disrepair. There are known to be 1,260 cleitean on Hirta and a further 170 on the other group islands. Currently, the only year-round residents are military personnel; a variety of conservation workers, volunteers and scientists spend time there in the summer months.The entire archipelago is owned by the National Trust for Scotland. News article: 'After a kill, some pray, some smoke': the man who shot the trophy hunters

In 1909, in British east Africa, now known as Kenya, the colonial government found a way of making a lot of money from poachers.

Tourist hunters had to pay a licensing fee in return for killing (and claiming as their own) the animals that plentifully roamed there. At the time, £50 would legally entitle you to kill two buffalo, two hippos, 22 zebras, one eland, six oryxes, four waterbucks, one greater kudu, four lesser kudus, 10 topis, 26 hartebeests, 229 other antelope and, if one wanted more, 84 colobus monkeys.

Under the licensing laws, trophy hunters could also kill as many leopards and lions as they could manage. The cats encroached on farms and killed livestock. As a consequence, they were classified as ‘vermin’.

Related: Finger on the trigger: trophy-hunters in Africa – in pictures

Hunters back then would have been aristocrats, the landed gentry. “Today’s hunters,” says the British photographer David Chancellor, “are hedge fund managers, doctors, attorneys, their wives and children.”

Over the last seven years, Chancellor has photographed modern trophy hunters, infiltrating the industry that caters for people like Walter Palmer, the dentist from Minnesota who, on 1 July 2015, wounded Cecil the lion with an arrow from a crossbow, tracked him for 40 hours then killed him with a rifle.

“I expected to take 21st-century portraits of people who would seem like 19th-century figures,” Chancellor says. “But they’re not. They’re the kind of normal people you hear on the news now.”

The series, he admits, has been profoundly disturbing. “I’ve photographed people who have hunted animals in the most callous way who are heart surgeons,” says Chancellor. “I photographed one man, an extraordinarily prolific hunter, who ran a pet cemetery business back home.”

What drives them, I ask, to exert such power over something so free? “It’s impossible to say,” says Chancellor. “It’s such a divergent cross-section: Some are meek-mouthed, some are forthright. Some will cry when they’ve shot an animal, some will pray. Some will drink beer or smoke a cigar. The only thing they have in common is the complete focus on what they’re doing. They don’t doubt it at all.”

Chancellor, who divides his time between Cape Town and London, took long journeys across South Africa for an earlier project on HIV. He became intrigued by the levels of privacy around the reserves beyond the cities.

“You would just see miles and miles of high fences – I wanted to know what was going on in there,” he says.

He remembers flying across the country, looking down from the window and seeing men walking across the plains dressed in head-to-toe camouflage.

“I wanted to discover best practice – the people who do this legally. As soon as I started looking into it, I was knocked over by the huge amount of revenue this industry makes.”

If the hunting industry began in the British colony of Kenya, it spread quickly, to Zimbabwe, Botswana and Namibia and, to a lesser extent, Zambia, Mozambique and Swaziland. Trophy hunting now occurs in 23 Sub-Saharan African countries.

Where once landowners would make their money from farming livestock, many now act as wardens for the ‘big game’ that roam their land. Foreign hunters are invited to kill such animals in exchange for a cut of the revenue.

And there are hordes of willing clients. In America, prospective hunters can attend ‘safari’ training schools, says Chancellor, where they practice shooting on remote-controlled elephants, leopards and lions.

“Many of the people who come to hunt have a place ready for their trophies in their homes, long before they even arrive in Africa,” he says. “They have expectations, and they must be met by the local industry.”

Chancellor recalls standing with an American huntress as she berated a local landowner. “You promised on your website that we’d see all the big five in a day, and we haven’t seen a lion. I want my money back,” she said. In general, though, he says “the huntresses were different to the male hunters. They would often spend a lot more time with the animals, both before and after the kill”.

Chancellor was also struck by how caring many of the professional wardens were about the animals whose lives they bartered for cash. “I think some difficult clients put them in very difficult positions, but I didn’t find a group of guys slaughtering animals left and right,” he says. “Many of them had a very powerful relationship with their environment.”

Chancellor has already gained notable success with the series, including the 2010 Taylor Wessing photographic portrait prize for the photograph Huntress with Buck.

The portrait, which remains one of the most striking in the series, shows a 14-year-old girl from Alabama – her name is Josie Slaughter – on her first hunting trip to South Africa.

With the bush behind her and the sky turning from day to dusk, Josie holds the deer’s antler as his body hangs limply over her horse’s neck.

“There was a contrast between the tranquillity of the location and Josie’s beauty and the dead buck – that was what I wanted to explore,” Chancellor says. “This intricate and complex relationship between man and animals, and how both struggle to adapt to their changing environment.”

It is, he says, an ongoing project, for the issue is only becoming more pressing.

To understand why they are called greenhouse gases, we need to first understand how a greenhouse works. A greenhouse is a structure made of glass or transparent plastic, which allows sunlight to enter and warm the interior. The glass or plastic traps heat, preventing it from easily escaping and maintaining a warmer temperature inside. This controlled environment is beneficial for growing plants, especially in cold climates. 

Similarly, greenhouse gases in the Earth's atmosphere allow sunlight to pass through and warm the surface of the planet. Once the sunlight is absorbed by the Earth, it is re-emitted as infrared radiation, which is a form of heat. Instead of allowing this heat to escape back into space, greenhouse gases absorb and trap it, thereby warming the planet further. This phenomenon is known as the greenhouse effect.

1. Carbon Dioxide (CO2): CO2 is the most prevalent greenhouse gas, accounting for about 76% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Carbon dioxide can remain in the atmosphere for centuries, making it a long-lasting contributor to global warming.

2. Methane (CH4): Methane is the second most abundant greenhouse gas, contributing to approximately 16% of global emissions. It is about 25 times more effective at trapping heat compared to carbon dioxide over a 100-year period. Methane is primarily released from agriculture (like enteric fermentation in livestock and rice paddies), fossil fuel extraction, and decomposing organic matter in landfills.

Sewerage floods the alleyway; on either side of the narrow passage are aging buildings. The stench of urine fills the air.
As we make our way into the night, I begin to make out shadows lining the side of the street. "Odijo, odijo," they shout.
Odijo is sheng (Kenyan slang) for teacher - it's an affectionate name they use for the man who has become something of a "messiah" for Nairobi's forgotten children.
Clifford Oluoch is a primary school teacher in Nairobi by day but has been spending his evenings for the last three months feeding street children.
"I was walking home one night and came across boys haggling for a cob of corn. I offered to buy them a cob each, more came, then more. By the end of the night, I had bought corn for 25 people," he says.
"They asked if I could come back tomorrow and do the same and I said I would. I've been keeping that promise."
The latest figures are difficult to come by but a 2012 Unicef report estimated that there were 250-300,000 homeless children in Kenya, most of them in the big cities.
According to Nairobi-based charity Kenya Children of Hope, 63% of the cities' homeless children have been on the streets on a part- or full-time basis for up to five years.
In the city centre, the vile smell of human waste, flowing near where we stand, mixes with a thick cloud of industrial glue - a drug of choice here.
There is a group of about 20 youngsters waiting crouching on the concrete.
Many of them are carrying small plastic containers - a few sniffs of glue can last for several hours.
It smells strong and potent. I gesture to it and ask one boy why he uses it.
"It makes me warm and makes it easier to sleep at night out here," he says, before drawing three quick pulls from the plastic bottle. I sense he doesn't want to continue with the topic.
His name is Thomas, he's 14 and has been living out here for the past four years.
Thomas says he has seen many people trying to help but says he thinks "Odijo" is different.
Some of the children here are from abusive homes, others left alcoholic parents behind.
But the streets are no picnic either.
"Life here is hard. Bad things happen, young boys get beaten up by the older homeless people and we fight for food," says one of the boys huddled around me, he too is sniffing glue and his eyes are blood-shot.
But they are mostly orderly and welcome me as Odijo's guest.
They tell me he is like their "messiah".
Earlier that evening, the teacher, his wife Benedette and their 13-year old daughter had buttered 30 loaves of bread. This type of meal costs about 2,000 Kenyan shillings ($22; Â£14) a day.
For months he has been splitting his salary between his wife and two children and 60 street children and says he was beginning to feel the pinch.
Thankfully word is slowly started to spread in his community - this month he got a donor for bread.
He says he can now use that money to see to other needs such as transporting someone to hospital, or helping some of the homeless women set up fruit stalls.
Still, this is an expensive project to maintain on a teacher's salary, not to mention the time away from his family - up to three hours every evening.
So why does he do it?
"My wife and I feel strongly about helping other people," he says.
"We know what is it to grow up having nothing. We know how difficult life is when you have no-one. This is making a difference, that makes all of it worth it,"  Benedette told me earlier.
It's dark now and he hands out the parcels quickly, desperate to get to the next location - for some this is the first and only meal of the day.
What took him and his family an hour to prepare is gobbled down in 10 minutes.
Some nights the feeding is followed by a counselling session - this is the most difficult part.
"A lot of these children have been disappointed so many times and that's made some of them hard. I've learned that they are just hungry for love - for someone who will care about them," he says, as if drowning under the weight of this task.
The children have a lot of faith in him - he tells me they make him feel superhuman, like he can solve all their problems. He, of course, knows he can't.
He has big plans to help get them off the streets - but with no-one else to help, that's a long way off.
We take a short drive. A group of mothers is huddled under a flickering streetlight near a shopping centre in the affluent Westlands district.
It's a busy area with fast-food restaurants. It smells of roasted garlic and warm curry - torture, even for me.
As Clifford makes his way to them, a crowd of children no more than three years old runs to him, tugging at the plastic bags in his hands. Another feeding frenzy.
"This is no place for children. I'm hoping to get the youngsters out while they still have a chance," he says.
One of the women tells me says she's been homeless for seven years and has no skills to speak of.
Her son, Wesley, just a year old, has a cold, so we walk to a nearby pharmacy where Clifford buys him medication.
The contrast of the woman and baby in their grubby clothes and the health worker in his crisp white coats is stark.
"They know I don't give them money. I don't encourage people to give them money either but if I can help with things like buying medicine then I do," explains Clifford as we walk out.
By this point the woman and her boy have disappeared back into the night.
Clifford has learned that the streets are addictive and that some people cannot leave - some do not even want to. This is all they know.
Being a Good Samaritan can be a thankless task as some sell the clothes he collects for them to buy drugs or alcohol.
But some - although few - still dream of a different life.
"I left school after my father died and my mother couldn't afford to take me to school, I thought it was easier to go out and take care of myself," says 13-year old Neville, who adds he wants to be a reporter.
"I want to go back to school one day. I'm hoping Odijo can help with that. I don't want to live here for the rest of my life."
Hearing this fills Clifford with hope and the drive to keep going.
"If I can save just one person, just one child, that would be enough for me," he says.
And so he keeps coming back, night after night with nothing more than buttered bread and a heart ready to love - and they are grateful.

response: This article narrates the story of Clifford Oluoch, a primary school teacher in Nairobi, Kenya, who spends his evenings feeding street children. Determined to keep a promise he made to these children, Oluoch uses part of his teacher's salary to provide them with daily meals. With an estimated 250,000 to 300,000 homeless children in Kenya, most living in big cities like Nairobi, Oluoch has made a difference in their lives, earning him the affectionate nickname "Odijo" or "teacher" in Kenyan slang. Despite his limited means and time, Oluoch hopes to help even more children get off the streets and improve their lives.

Providing a working model allows the USPTO to thoroughly review and analyze the device's functionality according to established scientific principles. By examining the model, patent examiners can verify if the invention merits a patent grant or if it simply defies accepted scientific theories.

This policy serves to uphold the integrity of the patent system by ensuring that patents are only granted to inventions that demonstrate scientific plausibility and practical utility, conforming to the United States Code, Title 35, Section 101, which outlines criteria for patentable subject matter. Kyphosis is a medical condition that affects the human spine, specifically the thoracic region, which is the upper and middle part of the back. This condition is characterized by an exaggerated forward rounding or curvature of the spine, often referred to as a "humpback" or "dowager's hump" appearance. In a healthy spine, there is a natural curve in the thoracic region that allows for flexibility, balance, and shock absorption. However, when this curvature becomes more pronounced than normal, it results in kyphosis.

There are several types and causes of kyphosis, including:

1. Postural kyphosis: This is the most common form of kyphosis, often seen in adolescents and young adults, and is primarily caused by poor posture and slouching. In most cases, it is mild and can be corrected through physical therapy and practicing good posture.

2. Scheuermann's kyphosis: This type of kyphosis occurs in adolescents during growth spurts and is thought to be caused by abnormal growth of the vertebrae, leading to a more rigid and exaggerated curvature. Bracing or surgical intervention may be required in severe cases.

3. Congenital kyphosis: This rare form of kyphosis is present at birth and is caused by abnormal development of the spinal column during pregnancy. Depending on the severity, infants may require surgical intervention to prevent complications and developmental issues.

4. Osteoporosis-related kyphosis: As people age, their bone density can decrease, resulting in osteoporosis. This can lead to compression fractures in the vertebrae, causing the spine to curve forward progressively. Treatment often includes medications to improve bone density and bracing to support the spine.

5. Degenerative kyphosis: This form of kyphosis results from wear and tear on the spine over time due to aging or conditions like arthritis that cause gradual degeneration of the intervertebral discs and facet joints. Treatment varies depending on the severity and may include pain management, physical therapy, or surgery.

Kyphosis can have various effects on the body, ranging from mild discomfort and cosmetic concerns to more severe issues like chronic pain, reduced mobility, and difficulty breathing. Treatment for kyphosis is primarily based on the severity of the condition and the underlying cause. In mild cases, conservative treatment options like physical therapy, postural training, and pain management are often sufficient. In more severe cases or when the condition is progressive, more aggressive treatments such as bracing or surgical intervention may be necessary.

Diagnosis of kyphosis typically involves a thorough physical examination, assessment of medical history, and imaging tests like X-rays, CT scans, or MRI to evaluate the degree of curvature and potential causes. Solve 80 = -27*f + 7*f for f.

Here we will solve the linear equation to find the value of f.

Step 1 - Write down the given equation:
80 = -27f + 7f

Step 2 - Combine the like terms (adding the coefficients of the f terms together):
80 = (-27 + 7)f
80 = -20f

Step 3 - Divide both sides of the equation by -20 to isolate f:
80 / -20 = -20f / -20
-4 = f

“My grandparents saved for the express purpose of creating a better quality of life for their children,” she said. “I am remarkably lucky.”

Her budget for an apartment, preferably in a prewar walk-up co-op building, topped out at $500,000. Having spent several years in drizzly London, she also wanted a high floor, for the light.

“I thought I was the only person crazy enough to enjoy walking up” so many flights, she said. She was in the habit, however, of limiting grocery purchases so she wouldn’t have to carry too much at once.

She knew she could get more space for the money in Morningside Heights than in the East Village. The neighborhood felt more adult, too. “The musicians that I know who live on the Upper West Side are much more mature,” she said. “They have families, they have kids, they have strollers, they go shopping at Fairway.”

Ms. Gang e-mailed an inquiry to an agent who had a listing for a large studio on the top floor of a co-op on West 109th Street. The price was $425,000; maintenance was in the mid-$700s. She was delighted when the agent turned out to be Nina Hennessey of Halstead Property, the wife of a drummer she knew.

That studio was already in contract, so Ms. Hennessey showed Ms. Gang another top-floor place — not a walk-up — on the 20th floor of a 1988 condominium tower at the northwest corner of Central Park. The asking price was $469,000; monthly charges were around $800.

“The views meant a lot to her,” Ms. Hennessey said.

Ms. Gang realized she did not want to leave the East Village after all: “I walk down the street and see people I know, which is awesome and it made me feel I was part of a community, and I didn’t want to leave that.”

Or as Ms. Hennessey put it, “She wasn’t going to feel at home anywhere else.”

Now the hunt focused on the slice between 14th and Houston Streets. Many places Ms. Gang saw were in disrepair, but she loved a small studio on East 12th. It was on the top floor of a sixth-floor walk-up, with a pretty brick wall and a beamed ceiling. The listing price was $297,000, with monthly maintenance in the mid $300s.

But with inventory low, Ms. Hennessey said, “the little postage stamp of an apartment went to multiple bids.” Ms. Gang’s offer of $306,000 was rejected. The apartment sold for $336,000.

Ms. Gang also loved a one-bedroom on the fifth floor of a walk-up on East 11th. The place was listed for $550,000, with monthly maintenance in the high $600s.

But if she spent so much money, Ms. Hennessey pointed out, “she wouldn’t have the assets-after-closing picture that is attractive to co-op boards.”

In any event, Ms. Gang’s offer of $515,000 was declined.

9. Pour the browned butter into a bowl: To stop the cooking process and prevent the brown butter from burning, transfer it immediately to a heatproof bowl using the spatula or spoon to scrape every last bit.

response:
Stainless steel is a popular material known for its corrosion resistance, rust protection, and low maintenance properties. To achieve these characteristics, approximately 11% or more of chromium is added to the steel. Chromium is the key element that provides stainless steel with its unique attributes and makes it more resistant to the effects of water, air, and chemicals than ordinary steel.

But what is it about chromium that makes stainless steel so effective at combating corrosion, rusting, and staining? Let's discuss this in detail.

When chromium is added to steel, it reacts with oxygen in the air to form a thin, invisible, and adherent layer of chromium oxide over the surface of the steel. This passive film is responsible for protecting stainless steel from external elements that might cause corrosion or rusting. The oxide layer is only a few atoms thick and acts as a barrier, hindering further reaction between the steel and its environment.

The chromium oxide film is self-healing, which means that if the stainless steel surface is scratched or damaged, new chromium atoms will come into contact with the oxygen, reforming the protective oxide layer and continuing to provide corrosion resistance. This self-healing ability is an essential aspect of the durability and longevity of stainless steel.

There are also other alloying elements sometimes added in smaller amounts to enhance the properties of stainless steel:

1. Nickel: Improves corrosion resistance and provides better toughness, formability, and ductility. It also stabilizes the passive oxide film and extends its resistance to more aggressive environments.
 
2. Molybdenum: Increases resistance to pitting corrosion and crevice corrosion, which are localized corrosive attacks that can occur in chloride-rich environments, such as seawater.
 
3. Titanium and niobium: These elements are often added to form stable carbides and prevent the formation of chromium carbides, which can lead to intergranular corrosion. By stabilizing the carbides, these elements maintain the corrosion resistance of stainless steel.

4. Copper: Enhances corrosion resistance, particularly against sulfuric and phosphoric acids, and imparts antibacterial properties to the alloy.

5. Nitrogen: Improves strength and corrosion resistance, and it is particularly beneficial in stabilizing austenitic stainless steels.

To summarize, adding approximately 11% or more of chromium to steel is what creates stainless steel and imparts properties that prevent it from corroding, rusting, or staining when exposed to water. The chromium reacts with oxygen to form a self-healing, passive chromium oxide film on the surface of the material, providing an effective barrier against corrosive agents. Other alloying elements may be added to further enhance stainless steel's properties, making it a versatile and popular material for various applications.

Bill Clinton takes to the Charlotte stage Wednesday night to do what he does best—talk . . . about the virtues of Democratic economics. Which means it's a good moment to remind everyone about the real economic history of the Clinton years, and why the results differ so much from those of Obamanomics.

Aside from Barack Obama, Bill Clinton is perhaps the Democratic party's most prominent figure. WSJ's Naftali Bendavid checks in on Mean Street, previewing Clinton's address to DNC delegates tonight. Photo: Associated Press.

In the nostalgic Democratic telling, Mr. Clinton got elected, raised taxes on the rich in 1993 to close the budget deficit and reduce interest rates, and thus kicked off one of the great booms in history. The truth is very different, starting with the fact that there really were two Clinton economic Presidencies.

Much like Mr. Obama, in his first two years the Arkansan bowed to the priorities of House Democrats and tried to govern from the left. He raised income and gas taxes while trying to impose a BTU energy tax, a government takeover of health care (HillaryCare) and a $31 billion stimulus, but putting off welfare reform.

Unlike Mr. Obama, Mr. Clinton failed to get his main agenda other than a tax hike through a Democratic Congress. This turned out to be an economic blessing for the country because it didn't weigh on growth, and a political benefit for Mr. Clinton, who didn't have to defend an unpopular agenda in 1996. Republicans rode opposition to the early Clinton agenda to take Congress in 1994, and that's when the second Clinton Presidency began.

Mr. Clinton moved sharply to the political middle. Remember "triangulation"? He embraced the goal of a balanced budget, using it to outmaneuver Newt Gingrich and Republicans over a government shutdown. After two vetoes and shortly before the 1996 election, he signed a GOP welfare reform.

As for economic growth, Mr. Clinton inherited an economy that grew 3.4% in 1992, including 4.3% in the fourth quarter. The expansion stumbled in the first nine months of 1993, no doubt in part due to the uncertainty of the Clinton tax hike. In 1994 stocks were flat and interest rates actually rose throughout the year, peaking on the very day in 1994 that Republicans took Congress. As the nearby chart shows, that's when the real 1990s boom began.

On policy, the rest of the decade was defined by a virtuous Beltway gridlock. Washington did little to interfere with private investment, and Congress even helped by restraining spending growth. Only toward the end of the decade did both parties began to spend like politicians again as surpluses rolled in.

Consider the policy contrasts between Messrs. Clinton and Obama. Under Mr. Clinton, federal outlays as a share of the economy fell to 18.2% of GDP in 2000 from 21.9% in 1992. Nearly two percentage points of that was from the post-Cold War cut in defense spending, but domestic spending also fell as a share of the economy.

For his part, Mr. Obama has presided over the largest spending binge since World War II, increasing outlays to 25.2% of GDP in 2009 and close to 24% of GDP for the next three years despite an economic recovery. Deficits have been above $1 trillion for four years.

Mr. Clinton did raise the top income-tax rate to 39.6% from 31% in 1993, and Democrats credit that with shrinking the deficit. But even two years after that tax hike, the Congressional Budget Office was estimating annual deficits of $200 billion a year. Only as rapid growth continued in the later part of the decade did the deficits vanish.

President Barack Obama and former President Bill Clinton in June

Meanwhile, Mr. Clinton agreed to cut the capital-gains tax rate to 20% from 28% in 1997. Revenue rushed into the Treasury as investors cashed in their pent-up gains.

Mr. Obama says he only wants to return to the Clinton-era tax rates, but he's already raised investment tax rates by 3.8 percentage points as part of Obamacare. Combined with the expiration of the Bush rates, that would leave some tax rates higher than in the 1990s.

Arguably the most memorable phrase (not related to a scandal) that Bill Clinton uttered during his Presidency came in his 1996 State of the Union address: "The era of big government is over." By contrast, Mr. Obama's four years have been spent expanding the government willy-nilly—with more spending, the promise of higher taxes, and intervention across the economy. His only economic plan now is still-more spending.

So as Mr. Clinton tries to lay hands on Mr. Obama and rewrite the history of the 1990s, the real story isn't how much policy the two Democrats have in common. What matters is what they did differently. Bill Clinton learned from the mistakes of his first two years. Mr. Obama has doubled down on his—and, on all available evidence, he will double down again if he's re-elected.

Scientific research, archeological exploration, and remarkable technological advances such as the use of robots to explore inaccessible areas continue to reveal new and exciting secrets about the Great Pyramid and its construction.

In conclusion, the Great Pyramid of Giza is the only wonder of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World that still exists today. Its durability, stunning architecture, and the many intriguing mysteries surrounding its construction, continue to captivate and inspire people from all around the world.

Among all new customers using Kindles or the Kindle app, phone readers are by far the fastest-growing segment, an Amazon spokeswoman said, declining to disclose figures. Among those who use the Kindle app, more people now read books on the iPhone 6 or 6 Plus than on any other Apple device, even the popular iPad Mini, she said.

To engage readers, publishers are now experimenting with ways to make the mobile-reading experience better. They are designing book jackets with smartphone screens in mind. (Handwritten scripts or small fonts may not be legible.) They are customizing their marketing materials—email blasts, Facebook posts and websites—to be read on phones. And some are trying to catch people on the go, offering free access to e-books in airports, hotels and trains.

“How do I serve something up to somebody who perhaps wasn’t thinking about a book two minutes ago?” said Liz Perl, the chief marketing officer at Simon & Schuster, which has teamed up with Foli, a mobile-distribution platform, to offer free e-books at specific GPS coordinates. “The read-anywhere option is amazing. It’s an obligation for us as publishers to find those people.”

Through the Foli mobile app, Simon & Schuster in May offered David McCullough’s “The Wright Brothers” free at more than 50 U.S. airports. In June, it served up “Yoga for Life” by Colleen Saidman Yee at the Solstice in Times Square yoga festival in New York. Now the publisher offers free e-books at hotels and airport lounges in New York, California, Missouri, Florida, Texas and Hawaii. Users can read as much of each book as they like free, as long as they stay within the prescribed geographical area.

Earlier this year, Penguin Random House introduced free excerpts of e-books on Amtrak’s Acela Express trains, including, naturally, Paula Hawkins’s “The Girl on the Train.”

Most people who read on their phones toggle back and forth between devices, using whichever is closest at hand when opportunity strikes, according to a survey this year by the book-recommendation site Goodreads. Nearly two-thirds of respondents who read on their phones said they did so because they didn’t have their e-reader or tablet with them.

Amazon, Google, Apple and Barnes & Noble all offer smartphone apps for reading books. They automatically sync all devices linked to the same account, so a reader can open an e-book on her phone and pick up exactly where she left off the night before on her e-reader or tablet. Amazon and Google recently introduced custom e-book fonts, both designed to be more legible on smartphone screens.

Fully 55% of all Oyster’s activity is now happening on phones, and the company in June introduced a new display option called Lumin that reduces the amount of blue light emitted from smartphone and tablet screens to make reading easier on the eyes at night (its users’ peak reading time). “I think people are reading constantly now, and it’s because of phones,” Mr. Van Lancker said.

Publishers are also devoting significant resources to developing apps that complement e-books and offer additional content from authors—from smoothie recipes and diet guidelines to “Curious George” games and daily affirmations inspired by the best-selling middle-grade novel “Wonder.” All are intended to keep mobile users engaged, and coming back for more books.

The literary world is divided over whether a phone can deliver the experience of deep, concentrated reading. Scholars who study the subject note that smartphones are an important part of the effort to improve literacy in developing countries where books and computers are out of reach for many people. Reading on a phone is better than not reading at all, these experts all agree.

But there is debate about whether the phone is appropriate for long-form reading, if other options are available.

With all their ringing, dinging and buzzing, smartphones are designed to alert and distract users, notes Naomi S. Baron, a professor of linguistics at American University and author of “Words Onscreen: The Fate of Reading in a Digital World.” Even when a phone’s alerts are turned off, your brain is still primed for disruption when you pick it up, she said. That could make a phone worse for reading than an e-reader.

“The phone is antithetical to deep reading,” said Maryanne Wolf, a neuroscientist at Tufts University who studies the reading brain. For most people, she said, a phone will make concentrated reading more difficult— though not impossible.

Anna Todd, writer of the “After” series on the serial publishing platform Wattpad, argues that phones are encouraging people to read more. Wattpad has 40 million monthly users—almost 90% of whom are on mobile devices. “People should stop worrying about how other people are reading, and be glad that they are,” said Ms. Todd, whose series generated 1.3 billion chapter views and a book deal with Simon & Schuster.

Many readers report being able to concentrate just fine on their phones. (Some turn off their alerts). On Twitter, people have celebrated major feats of reading, accomplished entirely on smartphones, including “Moby-Dick,” “War and Peace,” and “Swann’s Way.”

No one expects phones to replace print books altogether. And even avid phone readers acknowledge the devices have drawbacks. Many report feeling caught off guard when they reach the end of a book. They miss the physical sense of how deep they are into a book—and the feelings of accomplishment and anticipation that come with that. Others note that it is not as easy to share an e-book with friends as a hardcover or paperback. Many still read in print part of the time.

Laura Jefferson, 59, of Concord, N.H., reads on her iPhone for convenience —on the bus to Boston, in the doctor’s waiting room and eating lunch by herself at her favorite cafe in Concord. But when she knows she wants to lend a book to family or friends, she buys it in print.

Lloyd Miller, a musician from Brooklyn who reads on his phone and in print, used his iPhone to dip into Donna Tartt’s tome “The Goldfinch,” and found himself trying to read under his jacket in a Brooklyn movie theater, where he had taken his children to see Disney’s “Frozen.”

Mr. Miller, 41, said he prefers print, but downloads books on his phone for reading on the subway. He used his phone to read Hilary Mantel’s “Bring Up the Bodies,” and parts of Robert Caro’s fourth installment on Lyndon Johnson —which was too heavy to lug around. He also has his phone stocked with Beverly Cleary’s Ramona books and Judy Blume’s “Superfudge” series. Traveling around the city with his son and daughter, ages 7 and 10, the children often clamor for his phone.

He hands it to them, saying, “No games, but you can read a book.”

response: The rise of smartphone usage for reading is causing publishers to rethink the way books are designed, marketed and sold, with smaller screens in mind. This is leading to concerns about whether deep, concentrated thinking is possible amidst the ringing, buzzing, and alerts that come with phones. 2. There is a lot of pressure on the Sun: As a result of the gravitational force, the Sun's mass is extremely dense, particularly within its core. During this process, known as nuclear fusion, four hydrogen nuclei (protons) combine to form one helium nucleus consisting of two protons and two neutrons. A small amount of mass is converted into energy in the form of photons during this process, as described by Einstein's famous equation E = mc².

4. The energy from the reactions gives off different kinds of light: The photons generated in the nuclear fusion reactions are released as electromagnetic radiation. Consequently, their wavelengths become longer, transforming into other forms of radiation, such as X-rays, ultraviolet rays, and visible light.

The final step occurs when the photons, having reached the Sun's surface (photosphere), escape into outer space in the form of electromagnetic radiation, including visible light. Introduction

Whether you are a professional tradesperson, a DIY enthusiast, or occasionally engage in home improvement projects, having proper safety measures in place while working with machinery and power tools is essential to avoid accidents and protect oneself from injuries. This article offers a comprehensive guide on the appropriate protective gear to wear and safety practices to adopt while operating machinery and power tools. By adhering to these safety precautions, you can minimize the risk of accidents and ensure a safe and productive working environment.

The Importance of Protective Gear

1. Protective gloves

One of the primary risks when operating machinery or power tools is cutting or slicing your hands. This unfortunate incident can lead to severe injuries, infections, and even long-lasting physical disabilities. To reduce the risk of hand injuries, it is crucial to wear protective gloves specifically designed for the task at hand. Protective gloves can be made of different materials such as leather, Kevlar, or heavy-duty rubber, offering varying levels of protection against cuts, punctures, and abrasion.

2. Safety earmuffs

When operating power tools or machinery, one of the most overlooked safety concerns is the impact of noise on the user's hearing. Prolonged exposure to high noise levels during operation can cause temporary or permanent hearing loss. To protect your ears from loud noise generated by power tools, it is advisable to wear safety earmuffs. These hearing protectors help reduce the exposure to hazardous noise levels, ensuring that your hearing remains intact throughout the years.

3. Safety goggles

Eye protection is another essential safety measure to adopt when working with machinery and power tools. Dust, debris, and flying particles can easily enter the eyes, causing irritation and, in some cases, even blindness. To protect your vision, it is essential to wear safety goggles or glasses while operating any equipment. Choosing the right eyewear safety gear that meets the appropriate safety standards and provides a comfortable fit will ensure optimum eye protection.

4. Choosing proper attire

The clothing you wear while working with machinery and power tools should be carefully selected to minimize the risk of accidents. Loose-fitting clothing, for instance, can easily get caught in the moving parts of machinery, leading to serious injuries. Hence, it is crucial to wear fitting clothes that do not have parts that may get entangled with the tool you are operating. Moreover, wearing open-toed shoes poses a risk of injuries from dropping heavy objects, stepping on sharp items, or accidental slips. To protect your feet, it is wise to choose closed-toe shoes, preferably ones with slip-resistant soles and reinforced toe caps.

5. Securing long hair

People with long hair should take extra precautions when working with machinery and power tools. Long hair can easily get caught in the moving parts of equipment, causing severe scalp and head injuries. To prevent such accidents, always tie up your hair using a hairband, bun, or ponytail so that it remains away from the moving parts of the machinery.

Conclusion

Investing your time and effort in adhering to safety precautions will significantly increase your protection while working with machinery and power tools. By using protective gloves, safety earmuffs, safety goggles, choosing appropriate clothing, and securing long hair, you can mitigate potential hazards and minimize the risks of accidents, ultimately promoting a safer working environment. Remember that safety should always be the primary priority whenever you embark on any project involving machinery and power tools.

To give you a more comprehensive understanding, let me provide a detailed comparison between the two sampling techniques.

Multistage sampling and cluster sampling are both probability sampling techniques that are employed when studying large and complex populations. They are designed to make the sampling process more efficient and manageable.

Cluster Sampling:

Cluster sampling is a technique used when "natural" but relatively homogeneous groupings are evident in a statistical population. In this method, the entire population is divided into separate clusters, usually based on some shared characteristic or geographical proximity. The clusters should be more or less representative of the population. Then, a random sample of these clusters is selected for the study. All the elements within the chosen clusters are included in the sample.

For instance, if a researcher wants to study the academic performance of high school students in a large city, they may divide the population into clusters based on individual schools. Then, a random sample of schools is selected, and data is collected from all students in those chosen schools.

Advantages of cluster sampling include reduced travel and administrative costs and easier implementation compared to simple random sampling.

Multistage Sampling:

Multistage sampling is an extension of cluster sampling and involves multiple stages of sampling within the selected clusters. In this technique, the population is first divided into clusters, and then, instead of selecting all elements in the chosen clusters, further random samples are drawn from within each selected cluster at different stages. This process can be carried out in multiple stages, depending on the desired sample size and level of detail.

Continuing with the previous high school academic performance example, in a multistage sampling design, the researcher might first choose a set of schools (clusters). Then, within each selected school, a random set of classrooms or specific grades might be chosen. Following this, a random sample of students from within the selected classrooms or grades may be taken. This multi-step approach reduces the overall sample size while still maintaining a fair representation of the population.

Multistage sampling can increase the overall efficiency and accuracy of research findings while reducing the sample size and logistical challenges.

In summary, the main difference between multistage and cluster sampling lies in the additional stages of sampling within the clusters for multistage sampling. While both techniques involve breaking the population into clusters, cluster sampling includes all elements within the chosen clusters, whereas multistage sampling involves multiple stages of random sampling within those selected clusters to obtain the final sample. Each technique has its advantages and can be applied depending on the nature of the study, the required level of accuracy, and the available resources.
